title: Carrying tales
hook: telling someone what another said about them

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the Chafetz Chaim, and your line was keep thy tongue from evil. Who wants life? Did the question catch you mid-sentence? Today, the tale that travels between two people. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-one.

In Genesis, Sarah overhears a visitor promise that she will have a son, and she laughs to herself. She's old, she thinks, and her husband is old too. Then God speaks to Abraham about the laugh, and repeats what Sarah said. But listen closely to the repeat. God reports that Sarah wondered whether she, being old, could bear a child. The part about Abraham being old is gone. The Talmud, in tractate Yevamot, noticed the missing words, and it says God left them out for the sake of peace in the home. Today's word is what God, in that reading, chose not to do.
screen: `SARAH LAUGHS.` → `GOD REPEATS IT TO ABRAHAM.` → `ONE PART IS MISSING.`

segments.voice: Rechilut. Carrying tales: telling someone what another person said or did about them. Turn it four ways. First, the verse. Leviticus says: "Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people." Up and down. Going from house to house. Second, another peddler. Yesterday's peddler sold life. Rashi, reading this verse, connects the word for talebearer with a different one, the trader who walks from door to door with a pack. The talebearer works a similar route, as Rashi describes it: going into people's houses to find something bad, then telling it in the market. Third, what makes it different. Yesterday's book, the Chafetz Chaim, treats rechilut as its own kind of harmful speech. Lashon hara lowers someone in the eyes of others. Rechilut aims at a relationship. So-and-so said this about you. Your sister thinks you're selfish. The words may be accurate, and the person carrying them may even think they're helping. But two people who were at peace an hour ago now aren't. Fourth, what God left out. That's why the Talmud's reading of Sarah's laugh matters. The full report was available. It would even have been accurate. In that reading, God edits it for peace between a husband and wife. No one is asked to invent anything. The question is simpler: when you know what someone said about someone else, do they need to hear it? Or does the story only want a carrier?
screen: `NOT A TALEBEARER AMONG THY PEOPLE.` · `LIKE A PEDDLER, DOOR TO DOOR.` · `IT AIMS AT A RELATIONSHIP.` · `THE PART GOD LEFT OUT.` · then, large: `DON'T CARRY TALES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: set down one tale you're carrying. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself whether you know something someone said about someone else, something the second person doesn't know yet. A remark at work. A comment in the family. A screenshot. Let it come to mind. Now picture the two of them, still at peace with each other. Ask whether passing it on would protect anyone, or only move a hurt from one house to another. If it protects no one, picture setting it down, like a peddler putting down a pack. If you pray, you can ask for peace between them. The bell holds the time.
Rechilut. Carrying tales: going from one person to another with what was said about them, like a peddler with a pack. Today's word.
Your line: don't carry tales. Today, if you hear what someone said about someone else, let it stop with you, unless passing it on would protect someone. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Jews who study the laws of speech learn rechilut as its own category alongside lashon hara, and the tradition of editing a report for the sake of peace is often taught from the Talmud's reading of Sarah's laugh.
